gaps.detail: Cancels a job that has not started running. Against a real account the identifier could name a caller's own queued work, and a cancelled Batch job cannot be resumed — it has to be submitted again.
CreateQuotaShare is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free

Submits real, billable work to a job queue: AWS provisions compute for it and charges for what it consumes. Nothing in a scenario undoes a submission, and a probe group has no teardown.
Submits a SageMaker training service job — the same billable-work objection as SubmitJob, against a service whose training runs are the expensive kind.
Terminates a running job, killing its container mid-execution. On a real account that is someone's in-flight work, and the job cannot be resumed.
Terminates a running SageMaker training service job, discarding whatever the training run had done so far.
UpdateQuotaShare is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
UpdateServiceEnvironment is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Re-prioritises a service job that is already queued or running, which changes the order real work is scheduled in.
Replaces the security groups of a load balancer wholesale rather than adding to them, so a probe would strip whatever rules the caller's own load balancer relies on.
Puts a live load balancer into another subnet, which changes where it accepts traffic.
Takes instances out of service behind a live load balancer.
Removes a load balancer from a subnet, and with it every instance in that subnet.
Takes a whole Availability Zone out of a load balancer. AWS documents the instances in it as deregistered and the zone's capacity as lost immediately.
Adds an Availability Zone to a live load balancer, changing where it serves from and what it bills for.
Puts EC2 instances into service behind a live load balancer, sending it traffic it was not meant to receive.
Replaces the TLS certificate a live listener serves.
Replaces the policies applied to a backend port wholesale — an empty list removes every one of them.
Replaces the policies applied to a listener wholesale, which is how a listener loses its stickiness or its cipher policy.

Changes the console password of the IAM user whose credentials signed the request, which locks that user out of the console until somebody with the new password says otherwise.
Sets the account-wide sign-in alias. There is one per account, so the call silently replaces whatever the account already had, and every bookmarked sign-in URL for the old alias stops working.
CreateDelegationRequest is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Gives an IAM user a console password. It turns a programmatic-only identity into one that can sign in to the console, which is a change to the account's attack surface rather than to a test fixture.
CreateOpenIDConnectProvider is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Registers a SAML identity provider for the account. Everything the provider's assertions are trusted for follows from it, and nothing in a probe group removes it.
CreateServiceLinkedRole is implemented (Supported), so it may not be probed, and no recipe resource gives it a role
CreateServiceSpecificCredential is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Allocates a virtual MFA device with its own seed. AWS counts it against the account's device quota whether or not anybody ever enables it, and only DeleteVirtualMFADevice reclaims it.
Removes the MFA device from a user, so an identity that was protected by a second factor no longer is.
Removes the account's sign-in alias, breaking every sign-in URL built on it.
Deletes the account-wide password policy, so every complexity, rotation and reuse rule the account relied on is gone at once and AWS keeps no copy to restore.
Removes an IAM user's console password, locking that user out of the console immediately.
DeleteOpenIDConnectProvider is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
DeleteSAMLProvider is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
DeleteSSHPublicKey is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
DeleteServerCertificate is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free

Starts the deletion of a service-linked role. The role is what an AWS service uses to act in the account, so deleting it stops that service working, and the deletion is asynchronous — the call returns a task id and cannot be taken back.
DeleteServiceSpecificCredential is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Deletes an X.509 signing certificate from a user. Anything signing requests with that certificate stops being able to authenticate.
Deletes a virtual MFA device. AWS keeps no copy of its seed, so the device cannot be recreated and whoever enrolled it has to enrol again.
Turns off centralised root-credentials management for the organization, returning root credentials to each member account. It is an organization-wide security posture change made from one API call.
Turns off privileged root sessions for the organization's member accounts, changing what the management account can do in every one of them.
Turns off the account's outbound web identity federation, so every external workload that was exchanging this account's identity for a token stops being able to.

Associates an MFA device with a user and requires two consecutive authentication codes to do it. A probe would either enrol a device nobody asked to enrol or spend the user's authentication attempts guessing codes.
Turns on centralised root-credentials management across the organization, which takes root credentials away from every member account.
Turns on privileged root sessions across the organization's member accounts.
Turns on outbound web identity federation for the account, which starts vending tokens that name this account to external workloads.

Starts the account-wide credential report job. It is billed, it is rate limited to one report every four hours, and it collects every credential's age and last-used data into a report a probe has no reason to want.
GenerateOrganizationsAccessReport is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
GenerateServiceLastAccessedDetails is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free

A read, and the one entry here that is not about danger. AWS added GetAccountProperties to the model after every SDK the typed suites pin: aws-sdk-go-v2/service/iam v1.53.7 declares no GetAccountPropertiesInput, so probing it scopes this whole probe group away from go-sdk with go-emit-unsupported, and the java, dotnet and rust emitters — which read the model rather than their SDK — would emit a call those builds cannot compile. It takes no required member, so withholding a curated literal, which is what leaves GetRoleTemplateVersion refused, cannot reach it and this map is the only lever. Delete the entry once the pins carry the operation.
GetRoleTemplateVersion.TemplateArn (arnType, a string) has no bind, no matching export, no curated value and no derivable literal
Writes account-level IAM properties. There is one set per account, so a probe would overwrite the caller's own settings with no way to know what they were.
RejectDelegationRequest is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free

ResetServiceSpecificCredential is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Resynchronises a user's MFA device with two authentication codes, which consumes the user's codes and, on repeated failure, is what an attacker guessing them looks like.
SendDelegationToken is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Changes which version of a managed policy is the operative one. Every principal the policy is attached to gets a different effective permission set the moment the call lands.
Sets the account-wide STS global endpoint token version, which decides whether tokens the account mints are usable in Regions enabled after the call.

Activates or deactivates an access key. Deactivating one an application is signing with breaks that application immediately, and a probe cannot know which keys are in use.
Replaces the account-wide password policy wholesale. Unset members are reset to AWS's defaults rather than left alone, so a partial call silently relaxes rules the account depended on.
UpdateDelegationRequest is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
UpdateGroup is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Sets a new console password for an IAM user, locking out whoever held the old one.
UpdateOpenIDConnectProviderThumbprint is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
UpdateRoleDescription is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
Replaces the metadata document of a live SAML provider, which changes which assertions the account trusts.

Uploads a server certificate and its private key into the account's IAM certificate store. A probe has no key to upload that is not either a real one or a fake the account then holds forever.
Uploads an X.509 signing certificate for a user, adding a new way to authenticate as that identity.
Connects a custom key store to its AWS CloudHSM cluster or external key store proxy, which changes whether every KMS key in that store can be used at all.
Creates a custom key store bound to a CloudHSM cluster or an external key manager. Nothing in a probe group removes it, and an orphaned key store keeps its backing cluster associated.
Decrypt is implemented (Supported), so it may not be probed, and no recipe resource gives it a role
Deletes a custom key store. AWS refuses only while the store still holds KMS keys, so a store emptied by an earlier deletion is destroyed by this call.
Deletes the imported key material of a KMS key. Every ciphertext encrypted under that key becomes undecryptable until the same material is imported again, and AWS keeps no copy of it.
Performs an ECDH key agreement with the caller's public key and bills for it. It also takes a raw public key blob, which the IR cannot express.
Turns off automatic annual rotation for a live KMS key, which is a control an account's compliance posture is usually built on.
Disconnects a custom key store from its backing cluster. Every KMS key in the store stops working for cryptographic operations until it is reconnected.
Turns on automatic annual rotation for a live KMS key. AWS bills for each key version the rotation creates, and rotation cannot be undone for versions already generated.
Encrypt is implemented (Supported), so it may not be probed, and no recipe resource gives it a role
GenerateDataKeyPairWithoutPlaintext is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
GenerateMac is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free

GetKeyLastUsage.KeyId would bind to key.id, a value exported from a resource the run owns; a probe calls an operation the emulator does not implement, so against real AWS it would act on that resource for real. Add a curated literal for KeyId to values.json, or leave the operation refused
Replaces the key material of a KMS key with material the caller supplies, which changes what every existing ciphertext under that key decrypts with.
ReEncrypt is implemented (Supported), so it may not be probed, and no recipe resource gives it a role
Creates a replica of a multi-Region key in another Region. The replica is a KMS key of its own, in a Region nothing in this run looks at, and it can only be removed by scheduling its deletion there.
Creates a new key version of a live KMS key immediately. AWS bills for each version and a version cannot be removed.
Sign is implemented (Supported), so it may not be probed, and no recipe resource gives it a role
Changes the cluster, credentials or proxy configuration of a live custom key store, which can leave every KMS key in it unusable.
Moves the primary of a multi-Region key to another Region, demoting the current primary to a replica. It changes which Region may replicate and manage the key.
Verify is implemented (Supported), so it may not be probed, and no recipe resource gives it a role
VerifyMac is implemented (Supported), so it may not be probed, and no recipe resource gives it a role
Accepting a handshake is irreversible: it joins an account to an organization, or enables all features, and AWS documents neither as reversible.
A policy attachment takes effect immediately for every account under the target; an SCP attached to a root can deny actions across the whole organization.
Cancels an outstanding invitation permanently: AWS moves the handshake to CANCELED, and it cannot be reinstated.
Closes a member account. AWS suspends it immediately and permanently deletes its resources after the post-closure period; the account cannot be reopened.
Creates a real, billable AWS account inside the organization. An AWS account can be closed but never deleted, and it counts against the organization's account quota for good.
Creates a linked AWS GovCloud (US) account together with its commercial account; both are real, billable and permanent.
Makes the calling account the management account of a new organization. An account can belong to only one organization, so this either fails or permanently changes the caller's own account.
Declines an invitation permanently: AWS moves the handshake to DECLINED, and it can no longer be accepted.
Deletes the organization itself, along with every policy, organizational unit and setting in it. There is no undo.
Deletes the organization's delegation resource policy, which may be the only grant giving delegated administrators their access; the document is not recoverable.
Immediately withdraws an account's delegated administrator role for a service, and with it that account's access to the service's organization-wide data.
Detaching a policy takes effect immediately and can remove the guardrail every account under the target relies on.

Disables trusted access for a service across the organization. AWS documents that the service loses access to organization data, and that re-enabling it does not restore what the service removed on the way out.
Disabling a policy type in a root detaches every policy of that type from every target beneath it.
Grants a service organization-wide access and lets it create service-linked roles in member accounts.
Migrates the organization from consolidated billing to all features. AWS documents the change as one that cannot be reversed.
Enables a policy type in a root, changing what every account beneath it may do; the paired disable then detaches every policy of that type.
Sends a real invitation to another AWS account, which its owner sees and has to act on. Nothing about the call can safely miss.
Starts a transfer of management responsibility to another organization — an ownership and billing change the recipient can accept.
Removes the calling account from its organization. AWS requires the account to be able to operate standalone afterwards, and rejoining needs a fresh invitation.
Moves an account between roots or organizational units, which immediately changes the policies that apply to everything in it.
Replaces the organization's delegation resource policy wholesale; the document it overwrites is not recoverable.
Grants an account delegated administrator rights over a service for the entire organization.
Removes a member account from the organization. The account must be able to operate standalone, and rejoining needs a fresh invitation.
Terminates an in-flight responsibility transfer; the transfer cannot be resumed afterwards.
Mutates an in-flight responsibility transfer — a billing-ownership change already under way.

Deletes a secret's replicas in other Regions. AWS deletes a replica immediately — there is no recovery window for one — so the secret value stops being readable in that Region the moment the call lands, and nothing in a probe group puts it back.

Creates a copy of the secret in other Regions. Each replica is a separate billed secret that outlives the run, and ForceOverwriteReplicaSecret will overwrite a secret somebody already keeps under that name in the destination Region.

Cancels a scheduled deletion. Aimed at a stranger's secret it un-deletes something the owner deliberately scheduled for removal, and the recovery window is the only notice that owner gets before the secret goes for good.
RotateSecret is implemented (Supported), so it may not be probed, and no recipe resource gives it a role

Promotes a replica to a standalone secret and breaks its link to the primary. The split is not reversible — the two secrets diverge from that call onwards — and it is run against the replica, which is somebody's live secret.
Creates a namespace and, with it, a Route 53 private hosted zone attached to a VPC in the caller's account. The hosted zone is billed and outlives the run.
Creates a namespace and a Route 53 **public** hosted zone, which is billed monthly and answers queries from the internet until somebody deletes it.

Not refused for danger — it reads and changes nothing — but for what it could assert. Its whole response is one revision counter, and a counter read for a namespace that does not exist says nothing true about the service. It is covered instead by DiscoverInstances on the service the run owns.
Marks a live instance healthy or unhealthy, which is what decides whether clients are given it at all.
Rewrites the SOA record of the private hosted zone behind a live namespace, changing how long every negative answer under it is cached.
The same rewrite against a public hosted zone, where the cached answers are the internet's.

Adds a statement to a live topic's access policy, granting the named AWS accounts the named actions on it. Nothing in a probe group removes what it adds, and the result is another account holding rights over the caller's topic.

Registers push credentials (an APNs certificate, an FCM server key) as a platform application in the caller's account. The credentials are stored, the application is billable to use, and nothing here deletes it.
Registers a device token against a platform application, which is what makes a device a push target. A probe would enrol a device nobody asked to enrol.
Starts SMS-sandbox verification for a phone number, which sends a one-time password by SMS to whoever holds it. A probe would text a stranger.
Removes a platform endpoint, so the device behind it stops receiving push notifications. AWS documents the call as idempotent, which means it reports nothing when it has destroyed something.
Deletes a platform application and every endpoint under it, so every device registered against it stops receiving notifications at once.
Removes a verified destination number from the account's SMS sandbox, which stops the account being able to text it until somebody re-verifies it.

Opts a phone number back in to receiving SMS from the account after its holder opted out. Opting somebody back in is the one SMS action whose whole purpose is to override a person's stated preference, and AWS allows it only once every 30 days.
Replaces a live topic's data protection policy wholesale, so the redaction and blocking rules an owner relies on to keep PII out of a topic are gone the moment the call lands.
Removes a statement from a live topic's access policy by label, so whichever account that statement was for loses its access immediately.
Writes attributes onto a live platform endpoint — Enabled among them, which is what decides whether a device is sent anything at all.
Writes attributes onto a live platform application, including the push credentials themselves and the event-notification topics AWS reports delivery failures to.

Sets the account-wide SMS preferences: the monthly spend limit, the default sender id, the delivery-status role. These are one set per account, so a probe would overwrite the caller's own settings and could not put them back.
Completes SMS-sandbox verification with a one-time password. It is a write against the account's sandbox, and a probe guessing a password is the shape of a brute-force attempt rather than of a read.
AddPermission is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
CancelMessageMoveTask is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
RemovePermission is not a read operation; probes call unimplemented operations against a live account and must be side-effect free
